title: Listening Across
summary:
After the gathering in Alabama, and visiting the archives there and in New York, I realised that the conversation needed to shift (and quickly) towards practicality. With the support of the Faculty of Arts and Humanities at the University of Southampton, I proposed an interdisciplinary symposium bringing together scholars and practitioners across medicine, anthropology and the humanities, to begin considering how exactly a methodology like Endarkened Co-Composition could be applied here.
So on 19 October we gathered, in the room in Southampton and online, clinicians, anthropologists, musicologists and community researchers, around one direct question: if, when and how could this method work in clinical research? Not praise. Friction. I wanted the method tested by the people who would have to carry it into the clinic, the ward, the archive, the community. What came back were questions, sharper than the ones we arrived with, and the tensions between them, now drawn into a research agenda map: where the work would happen, what it would ask of each setting, where it might break. An agenda written together, out loud.
Its outputs, the research agenda and a co-authored position paper, are being shaped by the people who were there.

title: Workshop with Professor Evelynn Hammonds
summary:
Time in Provincetown with Professor Evelynn Hammonds, historian of science and medicine at Harvard University and a Project Associate.
“Workshop” is not exactly the right word. Really it was a prayer service, a litany and a kiki, all towards two archives at once: the archive of medical history as it pertains to Sims and medical racism, and the archive of Black women, of Black queer women in academia, traversing The Institution and leaving with our souls intact.
She graciously shared her home with us. She was expertly curious. And she makes the best quiche. Honestly, words fail.
We sat at her table and listened, and were listened to, which is its own kind of archive. How do you carry a history like this through a career, through The Institution, and still keep your ear open? She did not answer that. She showed us.

title: Research retreat
summary:
For the first major convening of this project, Dana-Ain, Lucy, Princess, Deborah and DW convened in Montgomery, Alabama. We spent two days at The More Up Campus, home of Michelle Browder’s Mothers of Gynecology monument to Anarcha, Lucy and Betsey. It was the project’s central co-production event, in the city where J. Marion Sims operated on the three women in the 1840s.
The days moved between listening, archival visits, making and speculating: sound-walking near where Anarcha would have been, time at the monument and at the marker for Sims’s office, conversations among collaborators, a deep dive into the ups and downs of Endarkened Co-Composition to understand the method, and Anarcha’s Seeds, a speculative storytelling workshop led by Deborah D.E.E.P. Mouton.
We ate goooooood, too. Food nourished our minds, and primed our ears and our imaginations. For we dreamed with Anarcha and with ourselves.
We drafted the project’s first research questions together and closed with commitments, to the work and to one another. DW McCrary filmed throughout for the documentary.
